title: CFA Economics: Business Cycles
subtitle: The four phases of an economy and how professional investors read the cycle's signals
openingQuestion: How many main phases does the business cycle have, and which phase does positive but slowing GDP growth belong to?
openingOptions: 2 phases: growth and recession; slowing GDP is a recession
3 phases: rising, stable, falling; slowing GDP is the stable phase
The business cycle has no fixed phases, varying randomly by country
explanation: The CFA Institute defines the business cycle as four repeating phases: Expansion (GDP rising, unemployment falling), Peak (growth at its maximum, with the first signs of overheating such as rising inflation), Contraction/Recession (GDP falling for at least two consecutive quarters on the technical definition), and Trough (the low point before recovery). GDP still positive but decelerating is the classic marker of late expansion, immediately before the peak.

realWorldExample.company: The Federal Reserve and the 2020-2023 cycle
realWorldExample.description: After the COVID-19 shock (an exceptionally fast contraction in 2020), the US economy rebounded hard (expansion in 2021), approached a peak with record inflation (2022), and forced the Fed into a run of rate rises to cool it down - a business cycle compressed into an unusually short window, with all four phases visible inside three years.

quiz.question: Which of these counts as a leading indicator, helping forecast the business cycle before it turns?
options: The yield curve, building permits, and consumer confidence
The consumer price index and average wages across the economy
Real GDP, the unemployment rate and quarterly corporate profits
Business failures and the stock of bad bank loans in the period
quiz.explanation: Leading indicators such as an inverted yield curve, building permit applications and consumer confidence typically turn BEFORE the economy formally changes phase - professional investors watch them in order to position early. Unemployment and GDP are lagging or coincident and report what has already happened, while prices and wages are slower still. Business failures and bad loans lag furthest of all, crystallising long after the downturn began.

quiz.question: During a contraction, which sectors tend to outperform the broad market?
options: Cyclicals such as cars, luxury goods and leisure travel
Defensives: consumer staples, healthcare and utilities
Technology and financials, because they rebound fastest
Property, because it benefits from falling interest rates
quiz.explanation: Defensive sectors have demand that does not depend on the cycle - people still eat, still see a doctor and still use electricity in a recession. This is the basic principle of sector rotation the CFA curriculum stresses in Portfolio Management. Cars and holidays are the first purchases households postpone; technology and financials lead the recovery rather than the contraction; and property gains from lower rates only once credit is flowing again.

quiz.question: What is the common technical definition of a recession used by the NBER and others?
options: The stock market falling more than 20% from its recent peak
Unemployment above 10% for two consecutive quarters
Real GDP falling for at least two consecutive quarters
Negative inflation sustained across two full quarters
quiz.explanation: The most widely cited technical definition (though the US NBER in practice uses a broader one, weighing several indicators together) is real GDP contracting for at least two consecutive quarters. A 20% drawdown defines a bear market rather than a recession; unemployment above a threshold is a symptom that arrives late; and sustained negative inflation is deflation, which can occur with or without a recession.

quiz.question: Inventories are building fast while retail sales flatten. Which phase does that signal?
options: Early recovery, when consumption is outpacing production
Mid-expansion, when firms deliberately stock up for demand ahead
The trough, as firms restart output after a period of cuts
Near the peak, just before the economy enters contraction
quiz.explanation: Unintended inventory build-up is the classic signal of a cycle peak: goods were produced on the old expectation while demand has begun to fall short. Firms respond by cutting output, and that cut is what pushes the economy into contraction. In early recovery and at the trough, inventories are being run down rather than built, and deliberate mid-expansion stocking is matched by rising sales rather than stalling ones.

quiz.question: Why do consumer staples hold up better through a recession?
options: Because demand for their products is barely elastic to household income
Because firms in this sector typically carry no debt and are therefore safer
Because they are allowed to raise prices in a recession to offset lost volume
Because governments usually subsidise this sector directly in hard times
quiz.explanation: People put off buying a car and put off a holiday, but they still buy rice and shampoo. Low income elasticity makes revenue in this group far steadier through the cycle - which is why it is classed as defensive in cyclical allocation. Staples companies do carry debt, they hold no special permission on pricing, and no government writes them a cheque; the stability comes from the shopping basket, not from policy.

keyTakeaways: Four phases of the business cycle: Expansion → Peak → Contraction → Trough, repeating over time
Leading indicators (yield curve, building permits, consumer confidence) forecast the cycle BEFORE it turns; lagging indicators (unemployment) report AFTER
Sector rotation: each phase favours different sectors - defensives in contraction, cyclicals in expansion
Technical recession = real GDP falling for two consecutive quarters, though institutional definitions such as the NBER's are more involved

practicePrompt.question: The yield curve has been inverted (short rates above long rates) for the past three months, while GDP this quarter still grew at 2%. How should a portfolio manager respond, on leading-indicator logic?
options: Ignore the signal because GDP is still positive, and hold the cyclical weighting as it is
Shift gradually towards defensives and cut risk, since an inverted curve leads the cycle
Sell the entire portfolio immediately, because a recession is certain within the month
Buy more high-growth technology, since the yield curve has nothing to do with the cycle
practicePrompt.explanation: An inverted yield curve is historically among the most reliable leading indicators of a recession (typically 12-18 months ahead), though never 100% accurate. Because GDP is a coincident or lagging indicator, the fact that it is still positive does not contradict the early warning - a professional manager adjusts the portfolio gradually towards a more defensive stance rather than selling out in a panic.

summary.keyIdea: The business cycle has four repeating phases (Expansion-Peak-Contraction-Trough); leading indicators forecast turns before GDP records them, and sector rotation is the investment strategy built on the cycle.
summary.commonMistake: Looking only at current GDP (lagging) and ignoring leading indicators such as the yield curve, which means reacting to a phase change far too late
summary.action: Track the yield curve and consumer confidence monthly to spot the signal of a phase change early

application.title: Applying this in CFA analysis
application.message: When analysing an economy for the CFA exam or for real work, always establish: (1) which phase of the cycle it is in, (2) what the leading indicators are signalling, (3) which sectors to overweight or underweight for that phase.
application.secondary: This is the theoretical foundation of top-down investing - one of the most widely used asset allocation methods in Portfolio Management.

sections.text: The business cycle is the pulse of an economy - understand it and an investor can position a portfolio before the market reacts, instead of chasing it afterwards.
The four phases of the business cycle

items: Expansion: GDP rising, unemployment falling, consumer confidence high, firms investing to expand
Peak: growth at its maximum, with the first signs of overheating (rising inflation, the central bank tightening policy)
Contraction/Recession: GDP falling, unemployment rising, firms cutting spending and headcount
Trough: the low point of the cycle, where conditions begin to stabilise before recovery

sections.text: Leading indicators change BEFORE the economy shifts phase - the yield curve, new building permit applications, consumer confidence, new factory orders. Coincident indicators change AT THE SAME TIME as the economy - real GDP, retail sales. Lagging indicators change AFTER the economy has already shifted - the unemployment rate, average lending rates. Professional investors concentrate on the leading set in order to act ahead of the market.
Sector rotation - investing with the cycle

Each phase of the business cycle favours a different group of sectors. In early expansion: financials, property and consumer discretionary usually lead (the cyclical sectors). In late expansion and at the peak: energy and materials tend to be strong as inflation rises. In contraction: consumer staples, healthcare and utilities (the defensive sectors) usually outperform, because their demand is stable. At the trough and into a new expansion: technology and industrials typically recover first as expectations improve.

sections.label: A note for the CFA exam
sections.text: CFA Level I does not ask you to forecast the cycle accurately; it asks you to UNDERSTAND the relationship between economic indicators, monetary and fiscal policy, and how asset markets respond in each phase - which is the foundation for Economics and links directly into Portfolio Management (asset allocation across the cycle).

Cross-check against coincident and lagging indicators
Rotate sectors to match the phase
